html:
The map's label for the peoples of the boreal forest of Canada and interior Alaska, shown from 1500 BCE to 1715. It is a land of spruce, lakes, rivers and long winters, too cold for farming.

Two great language families shared it. Athabaskan (Dene) peoples lived in the west and north-west, among them the Chipewyan, Tlicho and Gwich'in. Algonquian peoples lived in the east, among them the Cree, the Innu, the Ojibwe and the Algonquin.

Life followed the seasons:

  • hunting caribou and moose, and trapping beaver and hare;
  • fishing in lakes and rivers, much of it through the ice;
  • small family bands that moved through the winter and gathered at good fishing places in summer;
  • birchbark canoes in summer, snowshoes and toboggans in winter.

A hard winter could bring hunger, so sharing food and knowing the land were matters of survival.

Some Athabaskan groups left the north centuries before Europeans arrived and moved far south, where they became the Apache and Navajo of the Southwest.

From the 1600s the fur trade changed this world. French traders and, from 1670, the posts of the Hudson's Bay Company on Hudson Bay traded guns, metal kettles, cloth and beads for beaver pelts. Cree and other groups became go-betweens in the trade, while European diseases spread through the forest.
sum: The map's label for the peoples of the boreal forest of Canada and interior Alaska, shown from 1500 BCE to 1715. It is a land of spruce, lakes, rivers and long winters, too cold for farming.
